batchName: Empire: Claudius and Nero (AD 41-68) - Medium Batch 1

questions.question: How long did Claudius himself spend in Britain?
questions.explanation: Claudius crossed with reinforcements after the first fighting and spent just sixteen days on the island. Ancient writers claimed he brought elephants, a story modern historians doubt.
questions.sourceQuote: He spent just sixteen days on the island.

questions.question: What did Claudius's third wife do in AD 48 while he was away at Ostia?
options: Led the guard in a coup
Publicly married her lover, a senator
Fled to Egypt with his treasury
questions.explanation: She publicly married a senator; whether this was a plot to seize the throne is still debated. She was executed.
questions.sourceQuote: In AD 48, while Claudius was away at Ostia, she publicly married her lover, a senator.

questions.question: Where was Nero when the Great Fire began, according to Tacitus?
options: At the Olympic Games in Greece
In his palace on the Palatine
questions.explanation: Tacitus noted Nero was at Antium and left the question of his guilt open. Rumours nonetheless claimed he sang of the fall of Troy while Rome burned.
questions.sourceQuote: He noted that Nero was at Antium, on the coast, when the fire began.

questions.question: Why was Britannicus poisoned in AD 55?
options: He claimed the conquest of Britain as his own
He plotted with the Senate to kill Nero
Agrippina threatened to back him against Nero
He refused to marry Nero's sister
questions.explanation: Britannicus was poisoned after Agrippina threatened to back him. Four years later Nero had Agrippina herself killed.
questions.sourceQuote: In AD 55 Claudius's son Britannicus was poisoned after Agrippina threatened to back him.

questions.question: Where was the Roman governor campaigning when Boudica's revolt broke out?
questions.explanation: He hurried back from Anglesey but was too weak to save Londinium, a trading town just twenty years old, which he abandoned to be burned.
questions.sourceQuote: The governor hurried back from a campaign on the island of Anglesey in Wales, but he was too weak to save Londinium, a trading town just twenty years old.

questions.question: Who actually steered government during 'Nero's five good years'?
options: Nero's tutor and the guard commander
questions.explanation: Though Agrippina meant to rule through her son, his tutor and the commander of the guard steered government. Tax collectors were controlled more strictly, and slaves could complain of mistreatment.
questions.sourceQuote: But Nero's tutor and the commander of the guard steered government, and these years were later remembered as "Nero's five good years" (*quinquennium Neronis*).

questions.question: What happened to Nero's old tutor after the conspiracy of AD 65 was betrayed?
options: He was made commander of the guard
He was exiled to an island
He was ordered to kill himself
questions.explanation: The philosopher who had once written Nero's first speech was ordered to kill himself. The conspirators, senators and guard officers, were executed.
questions.sourceQuote: Nero's old tutor Seneca was ordered to kill himself.

questions.question: What did the Iceni king's will leave, a will that Rome ignored?
options: His kingdom to a neighbouring tribe
His treasury to the Roman governor
His kingdom jointly to his two daughters and Nero
His lands to the colony at Camulodunum
questions.explanation: He left his kingdom jointly to his two daughters and Nero, but Rome seized it. Tacitus says Boudica was flogged and her daughters raped.
questions.sourceQuote: Her husband, the king, ruled as a Roman ally and left his kingdom jointly to their two daughters and the emperor Nero.

questions.question: What did Claudius rule about sick slaves abandoned by their masters on an island in the Tiber?
options: They became free if they recovered
They were sold to pay public debts
They were returned to their masters
They were sent to serve the grain fleet
They became property of the state
questions.explanation: His famous ruling freed abandoned sick slaves if they recovered. Claudius loved law and judged many cases himself.
questions.sourceQuote: One famous ruling freed sick slaves whom masters had abandoned to die on an island in the Tiber, if they recovered.

questions.question: Why did Claudius's family stop his early history of Rome's civil wars?
options: It was too frank for them
It was copied from his tutor
questions.explanation: His history of the civil wars was too frank for his family, who stopped it and kept him out of public life. He still became a serious scholar, writing twenty books on the Etruscans.
questions.sourceQuote: His early history of Rome's civil wars was too frank for his family, who stopped it and kept him out of public life.
